name: Akim
title: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy
summary: Akim is a figure in the genealogy of the Gospel of Matthew, placed as a link in the messianic lineage from the Babylonian exile to Jesus' birth. As the son of Zadok and father of Eliud, he belongs to the third and final group of fourteen generations in Matthew's theologically structured genealogy. Although there is no further biblical information about Akim's life, his presence in this list testifies to God's faithful preservation of the promise to David through generations that otherwise remain hidden from history. Even the unknown links in the lineage carry forward the messianic promise. The name Akim (Greek: Ἀχίμ) is likely a shortened Greek rendering of a Hebrew name such as Jehoiakim or Eliakim, meaning "God raises up" – an appropriate name for one who stood in the line of the One God would raise up as Messiah.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus
keyEvents.description: Akim is mentioned in the genealogy in the Gospel of Matthew as the son of Zadok and father of Eliud. He is thus an important link in the royal lineage from David to Jesus Christ.

keyEvents.title: Part of the theological structure of the genealogy
keyEvents.description: Matthew arranges the genealogy into three groups of fourteen generations each. Akim belongs to the final group—from the Babylonian exile to Christ—a structure that underscores God's faithful guidance of salvation history toward its fulfillment in the Messiah.

versions.summary: Akim is a person mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew. He is the son of Zadok and father of Eliud, belonging to the generations between the Babylonian exile and the birth of Jesus. Although little is known about his life beyond the genealogy, he plays an important role in the messianic lineage.
versions.title: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy
versions.reason: [minor] Akim lived in the period between the exile and Jesus' birth. The epoch 'exile' refers to the actual exile period (586–538 BC), but Akim belongs to the generations *after* the exile. 'Intertestamental' would have been more precise, as he likely lived in the period between the OT and NT.; [minor] With 14 generations from the Babylonian exile (c. 586 BC) to Jesus (c. 4 BC), and Akim placed roughly midway in this sequence, c. 600–500 BC may be too early. An estimated period around 400–300 BC might be more likely, depending on generation length.; [minor] The term 'patriarch' is usually used for the great forefathers (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob etc.). For a person known only from a genealogy, 'ancestor of Jesus' or 'forebear in Jesus' lineage' is more precise.; [minor] There are four keyEvents, but they all refer to the same verse (Matt 1:14) or Matt 1:17. For a person known only from one verse in the genealogy, this could usefully be compressed into fewer events to avoid repetition.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. It would have been helpful to include a linguistic note on the name Akim (possibly a Greek form of the Hebrew Jehoiakim/Eliakim), as well as a theological note on Matthew's structuring of the genealogy in three groups of fourteen generations each.

versions.summary: Akim is a person mentioned in Jesus' genealogy in the Gospel of Matthew. He is the son of Zadok and the father of Eliud, belonging to the generations between the Babylonian exile and the birth of Jesus. Although little is known about his life beyond the genealogy, he plays a role in the messianic lineage that connects David's royal line with Jesus Christ. His name may be an abbreviated Greek form of a Hebrew name such as Jehoiakim or Eliakim.
versions.title: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is good but resembles the opening sentence of the previous version (version 1) quite closely. It should be rephrased to provide a fresher angle and avoid repetition.; [minor] The two key events overlap thematically quite significantly—both concern the genealogy. The second event adds some value with its theological structure, but the description in the first event also repeats the point about the fourteen generations. Consider making them more distinct.; [minor] The dating 'c. 450–350 BC' is highly uncertain and places him relatively early in the post-exilic period. Given that he is about ten generations before Jesus, a somewhat later date (e.g., c. 400–300 BC) could also be defended, but it remains speculative regardless. The note '(uncertain)' is appropriate.

versions.summary: Akim appears in the genealogy of Matthew's Gospel as a link in the messianic lineage between the Babylonian exile and Jesus' birth. He is the son of Zadok and the father of Eliud, belonging to the third group of generations in Matthew's carefully structured genealogy. Although no further information about his life is preserved in the biblical texts, his place in the genealogy testifies to the unbroken line from King David to Jesus Christ. The name Akim is likely a shortened Greek rendering of a Hebrew name such as Jehoiakim or Eliakim, meaning "God raises up" or "God establishes."
versions.title: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy
versions.reason: [minor] The time indication 'c. 450–350 BC' is very uncertain and may give the impression of more precision than is warranted. It might be more accurate to widen the range somewhat or clarify the uncertainty further, but this is acceptable given that it already states '(uncertain)'.; [minor] The second key event entry is more a theological observation about Matthew's structure than an event directly linked to Akim himself. Nevertheless, it serves as contextualization, though it could have been formulated slightly more clearly as context rather than as an event.; [minor] The third version should differ more from earlier versions. The information on the etymology of the name is a good addition, but the summary could be further enriched with theological reflection on God's faithfulness through the nameless generations.

footnotes.text: The name Akim (Greek: Ἀχίμ) may be an abbreviated form of the Hebrew names Jehoiakim or Eliakim, meaning 'God raises up' or 'God establishes'. Such name abbreviations were common in Greek renderings of Hebrew names during the Hellenistic period.

Matthew structures Jesus' genealogy into three groups of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the Babylonian exile, and from the exile to Christ (Matt 1:17). The number fourteen may have symbolic significance, as it corresponds to the numerical value (gematria) of the name David in Hebrew (דוד = 4+6+4 = 14). This underscores Jesus' connection to the Davidic royal line.

Several names in the third part of Matthew's genealogy (after the exile) are not found in the Old Testament. This suggests that Matthew may have had access to family lists, archives, or oral traditions that are not preserved in other known biblical sources.

During the intertestamental period (c. 400 BC – Jesus' birth), it was common among Jewish families to maintain detailed genealogical records. Such lists held great legal and religious significance, especially for documenting membership in specific tribes and clans, including the royal Davidic line.

Some scholars have suggested that Akim may be identical with Jehoiakim, who was high priest in Jerusalem after the exile (Neh 12:10,26). However, this is uncertain, and there is insufficient evidence to confirm or refute this identification.
